lines.text: Bronze drums and rebel sisters, emperors and colonists, long wars and a new beginning. This is the story of Vietnam.
Along the Red River, the Dong Son people of the Bronze Age cast great bronze drums, still a symbol of the nation's oldest roots.
Under Chinese rule, two sisters rose in revolt in the year 40. The Trung sisters are still honoured as national heroines.
In 938, at the Bach Dang river, a Vietnamese army defeated a Chinese fleet, ending a thousand years of Chinese rule.
The next year a Vietnamese kingdom stood on its own, the beginning of an independent Vietnam.
In 1009 the Ly dynasty came to power, and soon moved its capital to a new city on the Red River.
That city was Thang Long, the rising dragon, known today as Hanoi, the capital.
Under the Tran dynasty, Vietnam beat back not one but three Mongol invasions in the thirteenth century.
In 1802 the Nguyen dynasty took the throne at Hue. It would be the last, and it fell under French control.
France joined Vietnam, Cambodia and Laos into French Indochina, running plantations and mines for its own profit, while nationalism grew.
Ho Chi Minh, born in 1890, would found the Communist Party of Vietnam and lead the fight for independence.
In the north, a beef noodle soup took shape around this time. Pho is now eaten all over the world.
Vo Nguyen Giap, born in 1911, would become the general who defeated France.
In 1945 Ho Chi Minh declared independence. France fought to hold on, and war broke out in the year after.
In 1954, Giap's forces besieged and overran the French base at Dien Bien Phu. French rule in Indochina was over.
But Vietnam was divided. In the south, a state backed by the United States ruled from Saigon.
North and South went to war, a long and bitter struggle that drew in the United States.
In 1957 To Lam was born, who would become General Secretary of the Communist Party in 2024.
From the North, soldiers and supplies moved south along the Ho Chi Minh trail, through the jungles of Laos and Cambodia.
In January 1968, during the Tet holiday, communist forces struck cities across the South. They failed in battle, but American opinion turned.
That same year, American soldiers killed hundreds of villagers at My Lai, and many more Americans turned against the war.
US troops left in 1973. On the thirtieth of April 1975, Saigon fell, helicopters lifted the last evacuees from rooftops, and the war was over.
In the years that followed, up to two million people fled by sea. Many of these boat people never reached land.
The country was reunited in 1976, and Saigon was renamed Ho Chi Minh City.
Peace did not last long. In 1979 China attacked across Vietnam's northern border.
In 1986 came Doi Moi, the renovation: reforms that opened the economy to markets and began decades of growth.
Vingroup grew into the country's largest company, now building cars of its own under the VinFast name.
In 1994 Ha Long Bay, with its thousands of limestone islands, was named a World Heritage site.
And in September 2024, Typhoon Yagi struck the north, the strongest storm to hit it in decades.
From bronze drums to a booming economy, Vietnam's story is one of endurance.
